newsitem.title: FRANCE: Spending fall dampens French gov't hopes on economy.
newsitem.headline: Spending fall dampens French gov't hopes on economy.

text.p: French consumer spending took a tumble in June, highlighting the task facing a new Socialist-led government which hopes to bolster the economy by increasing household purchasing power.

Economists said the drop -- of 2.9 percent in June versus a revised 0.5 percent fall in May -- was larger than expected and unhelpful for an administration relying partly on faster economic growth to get its finances in order for European monetary union.

But they also pointed out that the latest figures had been adversely affected by a relatively small number of crucial Saturday shopping days, poor weather and a late start to summer discount sales at department stores.
Several economists predicted a pick-up in July, saying the discount sales appeared to have gone well and that a big drop in car sales since the ending of car-buying incentives may have bottomed out.

"The numbers are not good. We were expecting a one percent drop. I think it's a combination of things. There was an unfavourable number of Saturdays and bad weather hurt clothing, and sales started late," said JP Morgan economist David Naude.
"All these contributed to the fall but the drop is due to more than exceptional factors. Is it a threat to recovery? -- we don't think so, though consumption is a weak link in the chain," he said.
"The early indications for July are, however, for a strong month," he added.
Stuart Thomson, economist at Credit Agricole Indosuez, said the drop showed household consumption had fallen in the second quarter and that the year had got off to a slow start.
"Taking into account the bad weather and the working days factors means it is clearly not as bad as it first appears, and we should see a rebound in July and August," he said.
"But the problem is political as (the government) will have to base its tax estimates (for the 1998 budget) on these figures."
"The government desire for a consumer-led recovery has certainly been dented and it does make its task of reaching three percent (deficit as percentage of GDP) next year more difficult," he said.
"We've seen money being raised from the corporate sector and in order to raise extra money next year the government is really having to look towards the consumer," he said.
The government revealed the results of an audit of public finances on July 21 which showed the public deficit heading for 3.5 to 3.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn at the same time unveiled a 32 billion franc package of corporate tax hikes and other savings to knock 0.4 percentage points off the deficit and bring it closer in line with the Maastricht treaty criteria for monetary union.

Although the government has said the three percent target should not be read as meaning exactly three percent, he has also said reaching three percent was not impossible, if economic growth picked up speed in time later this year.
Strauss-Kahn says France's 1998 budget, to be presented in September, will be drawn up with the goal of getting the deficit down to three percent next year.
